newsitem.title: USA: Sequent shows its next-generation computer.
newsitem.headline: Sequent shows its next-generation computer.

text.p: - Sequent Computer Systems Inc said Monday it is demonstrating its next generation line of NUMA computers, which are capable of providing mainframe-class power to computers running Intel microchips.
The systems are designed to offer a low-risk alternative to customers who are moving from from legacy mainframe systems to open client/server-based systems, the company said.
Other companies also have developed NUMA-based computers, including Data General Corp, which has a pact with Unisys Corp.
Data General already offers NUMA-based servers running on Motorola Inc chips and has said it plans to offer Intel-based machines by the end of this year.

NUMA-Q is Sequent's version of the Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) design which allows client/server-based computer systems running Intel Corp Pentium Pro chips to distribute processing tasks across more than 250 processors at once, using a technique known as symmetric multiprocessing.
In contrast to competing technology called "massively parallel" computing, NUMA allows software applications to run on multiprocessor-ased systems without modifactions.

In a statement, Casey Powell, Sequent's chairman and chief executive, said that, "In November 1995 Sequent announced a significant investment to bring our new architecture, NUMA-Q, to market and we are delighted to demonstrate our fully functional Intel-based NUMA machines less than a year later."
Company officials have previously said investments in developing the new line of computers were behind the flatness seen in Sequent earnings during 1996.
Sequent said it planned to demonstrate the new machines at the Oracle OpenWorld trade show that starts here Monday.
